assessment.1. Existence of an interference: There was an interference with the applicant's freedom of expression. He wore a transparent visor bearing the political message smash capitalism during a public demonstration concerning the opening of the ECB headquarters, that is, in the core area of political expression in a protest context (see paragraph 6). He was then criminally convicted and fined for wearing it (see paragraphs 8-12). The fact that the object may also have had a protective function does not remove its expressive dimension. The Court generally treats slogans, symbols and forms of political protest used during demonstrations as expression protected by Article 10, and criminal penalties for such conduct amount to an interference (see nos. 68537/13, 29580/12).

assessment.2. Lawfulness of the interference: The interference had a basis in domestic law, namely sections 17a(1) and 27 of the Act on Public Assemblies and Processions (see paragraphs 17-18). The more difficult question is foreseeability. The legislative materials describe protective weapons mainly as shields, self-made armour, police or military equipment, gas masks or martial-arts items, while also noting that use of such items solely as symbols of opinion is not covered (see paragraph 19). Applying that notion to a relatively thin plastic visor with a political slogan, which the police did not object to during the demonstration itself (see paragraph 6), stretched the concept considerably. The domestic courts' reasoning was also not entirely convincing, especially the statement that the inscription itself showed the purpose assigned at manufacture (see paragraph 13). Even so, because the statute also broadly targets objects suitable and intended to ward off police measures, the interference was arguably sufficiently based in law, though only narrowly so (see no. 8080/08).

assessment.3. Legitimate aims of the interference: The interference pursued legitimate aims under Article 10 § 2, in particular public safety and the prevention of disorder or crime. On the same morning and in the same district, groups committed serious violence, including arson, attacks on police officers and others, and extensive property damage (see paragraph 7). In those circumstances, the authorities could legitimately seek to discourage the carrying of equipment capable of reducing the effect of law-enforcement measures and thereby emboldening violent confrontation. The protection of the rights of others was also engaged in light of the attacks on bystanders, emergency services and property (see paragraph 7; see also no. 23086/08).

assessment.4. Necessary in a democratic society: The interference was not shown to be necessary in a democratic society. Although the background situation was tense, the applicant himself took part in a demonstration announced as peaceful, wore the visor for about three hours, and there is no indication that he used violence or was about to do so (see paragraph 6). Crucially, the police neither warned him, nor asked him to remove the visor, nor excluded him from the event, even though domestic law expressly allowed such preventive orders and exclusions (see paragraphs 6 and 17). The later use of criminal law therefore does not appear to have been the least restrictive response. The domestic courts concentrated almost entirely on classifying the visor as a protective weapon and on the idea that the inscription was not its sole purpose (see paragraphs 10-14), but they did not carry out a convincing balancing exercise between the applicant's political expression and the concrete risk posed by his individual conduct. A criminal conviction, even with a relatively modest fine, is capable of producing a chilling effect on participation in political demonstrations (see nos. 29580/12, 68537/13). In these circumstances, the reasons advanced were not relevant and sufficient to justify the interference, and the measure was disproportionate.
